catalog_quote: While there are a handful of monosyllabic lexical items, most Malagasy roots are di- or trisyllabic. Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable. However, lexical items ending in one of the “weak final syllables” (-na, -ka, -tra in Merina; -ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952); -gnV, -kV, -trV in North Betsimisaraka (O’Neill 2015) and Tsimihety (Dahl 1952; Tsimilaza 1981) have antepenultimate stress, and a small number of words have final-syllable stress. The morphology is highly agglutinative, often resulting in very long words and stress shifts. O’Neill (2015) provides a phonological analysis of stress assignment and underlying forms; these details are not essential to the current discussion. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; roots ending in a weak final syllable (in Tsimihety -gnV, -kV, -trV with a harmonic final vowel) take antepenultimate stress; a small lexical set has final stress. Suffixation moves primary stress one syllable to the right; in compounds the rightmost member keeps primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 48: 'In longer words, certain syllables prior to the syllable bearing primary stress receive secondary stress'; in compounds the original stressed syllables of non-final members carry secondary stress (p. 49). Stated for Malagasy generally, not Tsimihety specifically.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak-final-syllable words (antepenultimate); 'a small number of words have final-syllable stress'; stress can be distinctive (MO tànana 'hand' vs tanàna 'village', làlana vs lalàna).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word) stress on citation forms; Howe separately treats phrasal accent (Sec. 3.8, 4.5.5). The Tsimihety-specific part of the sentence is attributed to Dahl 1952 and Tsimilaza 1981, i.e. second-hand; Howe's own recordings include ~25 Tsimihety speakers from Mandritsara but she does not restate the stress rule from her data.
new_statements.identity_note: Howe's sentence names 'Tsimihety' explicitly (her Tsimihety consultants were from Mandritsara and Mahajanga), matching Glottolog tsim1257 / ISO xmw; the default-penultimate clause is stated for Malagasy as a whole, the weak-final-syllable clause specifically for Tsimihety (after Dahl 1952 and Tsimilaza 1981). The primary descriptions (Tsimilaza 1981, Manoro 1983) are of Tsimihety proper.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.6 'Stress', p. 48: most Malagasy words have penultimate primary stress; words ending in a 'weak final syllable' -- given for Tsimihety as -gnV, -kV, -trV (citing Dahl 1952; Tsimilaza 1981) -- have antepenultimate stress; a few words have final stress; suffixation shifts stress one syllable right; secondary stress on syllables before the primary; compounds keep primary stress on the rightmost member. Her own fieldwork included ~25 Tsimihety speakers (Mandritsara, Mahajanga; word list Table C.5) but the stress rule itself is stated from the literature.
